Regulators tap position and SST power with DERs installed at the sites. 27 This report is available at no cost from NREL at www.nrel.gov/publications. 4.2 Value Analysis An economic analysis was performed to explore the cost-benefit of a MV SST with DC-to-DC converters to provide Direct current fast charging (DCFC) charge regulation to multiple charge stations as against a conventional distribution transformer with downstream AC-to-DC rectifier and DC-to-DC converters. In the latter configuration, the low-frequency iron core transformer provides isolation, the DC-to-DC converter(s) controls the charge voltages, hence current is applied to the EV batteries according to the chosen charging strategy, and the AC-to-DC rectifier delivers an appropriate power level to the DC-to-DC converter(s). [2] The standard MV SST configuration of interest has an active AC-to-DC rectifier stage that feeds a DC-to-DC converter which can regulate DC voltage and supply power to a power inverter. If there is no AC secondary load, the inverter could potentially be eliminated. For a single charging station, the SST could be tapped at the regulated DC terminal to provide regulated DC power to an EV. To manage charging to multiple DCFC stations, however, a corresponding number of smaller DC- to- DC converters would be needed. Since either the rectifier or the DC-to-DC converters can provide isolation, it may be more cost-effective to provide isolation once in the rectifier, instead of in each converter, simplifying the converters. The economic opportunity to be evaluated consists of three parts. First, there are savings to be realized by substituting the SST for a conventional distribution transformer, an AC-to-DC converter, and multiple regulated DC outputs, obviating the cost of the conventional transformer in its own housing, its concrete pad, and its secondary connections and wiring to the AC-to-DC converter. Second, the expense of conventional transformer power losses will be avoided; the power electronics losses in the respective configurations will be roughly equivalent. Finally, there may be avoided costs through use of the MV SST’s capability to provide reactive power onto the distribution system–a capability that is not typically available from behind-the-meter or secondary voltage power electronics in the configuration using the conventional transformer.
